summary: POC scoping focused on how Aurelia will integrate their variable client scripts with Redwood's benchmark harness. Key success criteria: 95th percentile latency target for streaming and non-streaming paths, end-to-end throughput for peak clinic hours, golden prompt fidelity and regression tolerance. Decided to run two parallel baseline runs: a streaming-first run and a batched non-streaming run to compare latency/cost tradeoffs.
transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-07-12
Start: 16:00 UTC
Duration: 57 minutes
Attendees: Samira Patel, Marcus Lee, Jordan Kim (Redwood) — Diane Brooks, Carlos Mendez, Priya Sharma, Tom Nguyen (Aurelia)

Auto-summary (auto-generated, may be incomplete): Discussed POC scope and acceptance criteria, sharing harness scripts, decision to run paired streaming vs batch benchmarks, security checklist items.

[00:00] Samira: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, I'm Samira from Redwood — that's Marcus the SE and Jordan on CSM. Thanks for taking the time. Diane, do you want to kick off with a quick context on Aurelia's use case?

[00:18] Diane: Sure, real quick: we're building a clinical note assistant used by nurses during intake. It's behind our internal app, so low latency during peak hours matters. We have a mix of short prompts (one-liners) and longer multi-turn notes. Our current thing is on-prem transformer endpoints but costs are spiky and reliability not great. We're evaluating Redwood POC to see if we can migrate inferencing while keeping latency and privacy requirements.

[00:44] Marcus: Got it. When you say short prompts vs long multi-turn, any numbers — tokens per request or distribution?

[00:52] Diane: Typical short is 20–50 tokens, long is 400–1,200 tokens. About 65% of requests are short, but the long ones happen during charting windows and are latency-sensitive too.

[01:12] Carlos: Also want to flag that we have a strict PHI handling policy, so KMS + customer-managed keys are mandatory. We also need audit logs for model inputs for compliance.

[01:28] Samira: Absolutely. Redwood Private supports customer KMS and audit logs; we'll include the security checklist later. For the POC harness we can redact or hash PII before sending, or run in VPC if you want to avoid egress — both possible.

[01:43] Priya: For success criteria, product is asking for 95th percentile latency under 450 ms for short prompts, and for long prompts a 95th under 2.2 s — is that realistic?

[01:58] Marcus: That's aggressive but might be achievable with streaming for long prompts and optimized KV cache for repeated prefixes. The short prompts target is doable on a dedicated capacity plan depending on model choice and batch size. We'll need to baseline with your real scripts.

[02:16] Tom: Quick Q: do we have to rewrite our client scripts to stream, or can the harness accommodate non-streaming with similar telemetry?

[02:26] Marcus: The harness supports both. We provide a small adapter pattern — you drop in your client requests and the harness can run a streaming path and a non-streaming batched path. We do recommend minimal changes to enable chunked streaming if you want early token emission. But we can emulate streaming from non-streaming by slicing requests — though that affects fidelity.

[02:48] Diane: We care about fidelity, we don't want hallucination shifts between stream vs batch.

[02:54] Marcus: Totally. That's why we run paired runs with identical prompt sets and also capture token-level divergence metrics. We'll compute ROUGE-like overlap and a custom golden-response diff.

[03:12] [00:03:12] Speaker 3: (murmurs)

[03:20] Samira: Let's walk through the proposed POC phases: 1) onboarding + small smoke run with 2000 requests to validate adapter and security; 2) parallel benchmarks — a streaming run using your client scripts as-is and a batched non-streaming run with the harness' batching behavior; 3) acceptance runs for SLA verification across peak-hour replay. Does that align?

[03:45] Diane: Yes. How long will each phase take?

[03:49] Jordan: Onboarding + smoke we can do in 3 business days after we get scripts and firewall config. Benchmarks we typically run two 24–48 hour windows to capture variability and tail latency — so total POC ~3 weeks including analysis.

[04:08] Carlos: Firewall config — we need a list of IPs and ports. Also outbound-only? We prefer outbound-only for security.

[04:17] Marcus: We'll provide ephemeral egress ranges for the Dedicated cluster or for Private peering we can do VPC peering — whichever you prefer. For outbound-only, we can use NAT and a small set of IPs. I'll add that to the action items.

[04:30] Tom: On workload sizing — what's the throughput we should target for bench runs? We have about 120 RPS at peak for short prompts spread across 30 clinics. That spikes to ~400 concurrent long-deferred charting requests during evening batch windows.

[04:48] Marcus: Good to know. For the POC we'll emulate peak and a pre-peak baseline. Proposed: baseline at 50 RPS short + 10 long; peak at 120 RPS short + 60 concurrent long (modeling concurrency not just RPS). We'll scale up if the first run shows headroom.

[05:09] Priya: And what about token budget / cost modeling? We need to estimate monthly spend if we go production.

[05:16] Samira: We'll produce a unit cost model after the benchmark: tokens-per-request distribution * measured cost-per-token under your selected model/quantization. We'll also show cost delta for streaming vs non-streaming because streaming can reduce perceived latency but may increase total tokens if clients re-request prefixes.

[05:39] Diane: Can you summarize what you need from us to get started?

[05:44] Marcus: Sure: 1) representative script set (24–48 hour capture) with golden prompts flagged; 2) expected RPS and concurrency profiles (you gave peaks, we want minute-level histogram if possible); 3) network firewall rules or VPC peering preference; 4) decision on whether golden prompts can be synthetic if PHI is sensitive — we can accept redacted copies but need fidelity-preserving redaction guidance.

[06:12] Diane: We'll redact and provide synthetic placeholders for sensitive fields; Diane will own that.

[06:18] [00:06:18] Speaker 2: (crosstalk)

[06:25] Carlos: On metrics — besides p95 latency and total throughput what else should we capture? Error rates, retries, tokenization variance, and KV cache hit ratio. Also the end-to-end ingress-to-client latency including network hop.

[06:40] Marcus: We'll instrument those. The harness emits per-request metadata: request_id, start_ts, first_token_ts, last_token_ts, model_variant, batch_id, kv_cache_hit (true/false), tokens_in, tokens_out, and a small trace id for distributed tracing. We can ship traces to your OpenTelemetry collector or to Redwood Console for the POC.

[07:06] Tom: How do you handle streaming fallbacks if a model variant falls back mid-request? We saw issues in our current stack where fallback caused duplication.

[07:16] Marcus: Redwood has a deterministic fallback policy. For POC we'll run with a single pinned model per path so we avoid mixed model mid-request. If we test fallback we do so with controlled failure injection so we can observe dedup logic. We'll share the runbook.

[07:34] Priya: On fidelity checks, you mentioned golden-response diffs. How tolerant are you to token-level differences?

[07:42] Marcus: We compute normalized token edit distance and show example flags. For acceptance we typically allow small token-level differences if semantic similarity is above a threshold and no medical hallucination is introduced. Diane, since this is clinical you might set a stricter gating.

[07:58] Diane: We'll need near-zero hallucination. If any hallucination occurs in a clinical fact, it's a fail for that prompt. Non-clinical wording changes are tolerable.

[08:08] Samira: Noted — we'll make that explicit in the acceptance criteria doc.

[08:13] [00:08:13] Speaker 4: (typing)

[08:20] Marcus: One more technical note: KV/prefix caching will help multi-turn sessions. If you have common prefixes in templates used by clinicians, caching can reduce cost and latency significantly. Share examples and we can suggest caching policies.

[08:36] Tom: We do have templates — about 25 canonical templates. We'll include those in the script set.

[08:42] Diane: Licensing question: if we move to Redwood Dedicated do we get model quantization options? We use smaller quantized models internally to save cost.

[08:53] Samira: Yes. Dedicated supports multiple model variants and we provide quantized variants where applicable. Our Optimize team will recommend quantization profiles based on your workload. We'll include a cost-quality curve in the post-benchmark report.

[09:08] Carlos: Security: we need SSO + SAML, RBAC for team members, and audit logs retention policy. Also will you allow bring-your-own-key?

[09:18] Jordan: We support SSO/SAML and per-token auditing. BYOK via customer-managed KMS is supported in Private. We'll attach the SOC2/ISO docs to the repo.

[09:30] Diane: Great. Any blockers you foresee?

[09:34] Marcus: Only getting the scripts and the network config quickly. Also a small wrinkle: if your scripts rely on session affinity across multiple backend copies, we need to emulate sticky routing or ensure KV cache is global for the session; we'll advise on adapter config.

[09:53] Samira: Let's talk about acceptance criteria concretely so everyone is aligned. Proposed acceptance checklist: 1) p95 latency short prompts <= 450 ms for streaming or <= 350 ms for non-streaming batched path? Actually that sounds inverted — we should set concrete values: p95 short-stream <= 350 ms, p95 short-batch <= 450 ms, p95 long-stream <= 2.2s, p95 long-batch <= 3.8s. 2) end-to-end error rate < 0.5% during peak. 3) no clinically incorrect hallucinations in golden prompts. 4) documented cost model and monthly estimate within 15% of target. 5) KV cache hit ratio >= 60% for templated flows. Thoughts?

[10:38] Priya: Those numbers help; can we relax short-batch to 500 ms? Client engineering prefers slightly higher for batch but wants consistent tail.

[10:48] Marcus: We can do 500 ms for short-batch during POC acceptance, but we'll note production SLA differences.

[10:54] Diane: We'll accept with short-stream p95 <= 350 ms, short-batch p95 <= 500 ms, long-stream <= 2.2 s, long-batch <= 4.0 s. Error rate < 0.5% and 0 clinical hallucinations in golden set.

[11:14] Samira: Excellent. I'll write those into the acceptance doc and send around.

[11:20] [00:11:20] Speaker 1: (laughter)

[11:26] Marcus: On harness integration specifics — we have a python adapter and a Java/Node example. Which tech stack are you planning to run from?

[11:35] Tom: Node for the front-end adapter and a Go-based backend. We can run the harness adapter in a docker container that calls your endpoint.

[11:42] Marcus: Perfect. We'll provide a docker-compose sample and a small CI job that runs a smoke test on merge. The harness will accept a CSV of client requests or a small Kafka replay if you prefer streaming the traffic.

[11:56] Priya: Kafka replay might be better to capture realistic client timing for peak.

[12:01] Marcus: We support Kafka replay; we'll need a sample topic schema and a short-lived test cluster credentials for the run.

[12:08] Diane: One tricky bit is that our current telemetry strips timestamps occasionally. We can add a minimal trace ID to help correlation for the POC.

[12:16] Marcus: Great. Correlation id helps a lot.

[12:20] Samira: Anything else on the technical side?

[12:23] Carlos: Just to confirm: streaming vs batch will be run on the same hardware profile to make cost/latency apples-to-apples?

[12:31] Marcus: Correct — we'll run both on the same Dedicated node sizes. We'll also run a second variant with quantized model to see cost impact.

[12:40] Diane: Sounds good. Timeline recap?

[12:44] Jordan: Day 0 (after artifacts): smoke run within 3 business days. Two parallel 48-hour benchmark windows over next 10 calendar days. Analysis and cost model within 5 days post-run. Total ~3 weeks.

[12:59] Samira: I'll send a calendar invite for a kickoff and include the acceptance criteria doc. Marcus will drop the harness examples in the repo.

[13:08] [00:13:08] Speaker 2: (background noise)

[13:15] Priya: Quick ask: can the harness produce anonymized transcripts for the golden prompts so we can review offline?

[13:22] Marcus: Yes, we can redact PII and produce anonymized golden diffs. We'll demonstrate that in the smoke run.

[13:32] Diane: One last thing — who owns the post-POC handoff to production? We want a single path to go from Redwood Dedicated to our infra.

[13:40] Samira: Jordan (CSM) will coordinate handoff, and we'll include runbooks for migration and autoscaling config. We'll also propose a pilot reserved capacity plan if the benchmark meets acceptance.

[13:51] Tom: OK great. Appreciate the clear plan.

[13:55] Samira: To wrap up — agreed action items and next steps as Samira/Jordan outlined. We'll target the smoke run within three business days after we receive artifacts. Anything else?

[14:07] Diane: No, that's it. Thanks everyone.

[14:10] Samira: Thanks all. We'll follow up by email with the repo link, pricing, and the kickoff invite.

End of transcript.

Notes: transcript contains typical ASR artifacts and occasional misattribution; timestamps roughly every 30–90 seconds.
